scenes.heading: indentation
scenes.caption: Indentation is the spaces at the start of a line that show which lines belong inside a function, a loop, or a condition. In Python, indentation is syntax. A wrong indent changes which lines run, or the file will not run at all. In other languages it is still how humans see structure.

items: Indentation is the spaces at the start of a line that show which lines belong inside a function, a loop, or a condition

scenes.heading: Step by step: indentation
scenes.caption: Pick one width, usually four spaces, and do not mix in tabs. Everything inside a block lines up. When the block ends, step back out. Let the editor do it, then read the shape.

items: Pick one width, usually four spaces, and do not mix in tabs.

scenes.heading: comments
scenes.caption: A comment is a note in the source that the program does not run. It should say why, not repeat what the next line already says. Comments that restate the code go stale and then lie. A comment that explains a constraint saves the next person from “fixing” it.

items: A comment is a note in the source that the program does not run

Comments that restate the code go stale and then lie. A comment that explains a constraint saves the next person from “fixing” it

scenes.heading: Step by step: comments
scenes.caption: Do not comment name = name + 1. Do comment a rule that is not visible, such as a limit imposed by another system. Delete comments that no longer match the code. Prefer a clearer name over a comment that translates a bad one.

items: Do not comment name = name + 1.

scenes.heading: Variables

scenes.heading: Scope
scenes.caption: Scope is the region of the program where a name can be seen. A name created inside a function is usually invisible outside it. Scope is why two functions can both use a variable called count and not smash each other.

items: Scope is the region of the program where a name can be seen
A name created inside a function is usually invisible outside it
Scope is why two functions can both use a variable called count and not smash each other

scenes.heading: Step by step: Scope
scenes.caption: Notice where the name is created. Inside that block, the name is visible. Outside that block, it is not, unless you passed it or returned it. When two names match, the nearest enclosing one wins.

items: Notice where the name is created.
Inside that block, the name is visible.
Outside that block, it is not, unless you passed it or returned it.
When two names match, the nearest enclosing one wins.

scenes.heading: Detail: Scope
scenes.caption: A loop variable is often scoped to the loop. Using it after the loop is a common bug in some languages and a design smell in all of them.

items: A loop variable is often scoped to the loop. Using it after the loop is a common bug in some languages and a design smell in all of them.

scenes.heading: Inheritance
scenes.caption: Inheritance lets a new class start from an existing class and then add or replace behaviour. The new class is the child. The existing one is the parent. It is useful when several types really are the same kind of thing with a twist. It is harmful when you use it only to reuse a few lines.

scenes.heading: Polymorphism
scenes.caption: Polymorphism means you can call the same action on different types, and each type does the version that is right for it. The caller does not have to know the exact type. It is how you write one loop that draws shapes, charges payments, or saves records, while each kind of thing keeps its own details.

scenes.heading: Decorators
scenes.caption: A decorator is a function that wraps another function to add behaviour, such as logging or access checks, without copying that behaviour into every function. The wrapper must look like the original function to callers: same arguments, same return, and a preserved name if tools inspect it.

scenes.heading: Authentication basics
scenes.caption: Authentication answers “who is this? ”. The user proves identity, often with a password, a code, or a signed token. It is not the same as authorisation, which answers “what may this person do? ”. You need both, in that order.
